The Colour of the Sun follows two teens—one Ryukyu, the island’s indigenous culture, and an American living on the base—navigating a complicated relationship. “The backdrop is a little darker,” Tera says, “because obviously the military brings a lot of issues in Okinawa. So that creates a shadow over this friendship, where we see this generational trauma that comes and changes the perception of these two kids toward each other.”

A few days ahead of the premiere, Harris and Tera were spending plenty of time with their film’s young cast, some of whom had never left Okinawa before. “Our star, Naoto [Shimajiri], was standing at the airport in front of a guy who had a sign with his name on it, and he had no idea that it was for him,” Harris says. “He thought we would be there to pick him up.”
https://media.gq.com/photos/6aa4187f3c72e1caf42c77bc/master/w_1600%2Cc_limit/11-46940028.jpg

Despite that greenness, Harris and Tera had already seen flashes of readiness for the spotlight in their actors—particularly during a fitting for the Maison Margiela looks they’d all be wearing at the festival. “Once they put on the clothes, it was so cool to see how quickly they were able to ease into being movie stars,” Harris says. “There was no hesitation. It was like all of a sudden I saw Yuma [Taira] just putting her hands like this and standing on the carpet already in her head.”

Tera says that Margiela (whose team he also first met through GQ Japan) felt like the perfect choice to represent The Colour of the Sun, which was filmed entirely on 35 millimeter. “Margiela has always been so great at pushing for different textures, and the film is very much about that visually,” he says.

“A movie premiere is a moment when everyone gets to be in a band together,” Harris adds. “You want the band to all show up looking right and playing their parts properly, so you need a designer that is dynamic enough to really show off all of the different colors of the players in your band.” Unsurprisingly, when the crew hit the red carpet on Wednesday night—all glammed up in hair and make-up by Giovanni Errol—their luscious mix of velvets and tweeds and silks looked supremely rock-’n’-roll. (Today, the film was awarded the prestigious FIPRESCI International Critics Prize.)

“This story is just going to be an advertisement about how GQ changes lives,” Jeremy O. Harris says, laughing over Zoom.

The acclaimed playwright is seated next to photographer-turned-filmmaker Xavier Tera in the light-drenched living room of a gilded Venetian palazzo. The pair are in town for the Venice Film Festival premiere of Tera’s feature debut, The Colour of the Sun, which Harris produced alongside Jane Chartier, Stella Savino, and Shogen. It’s the culmination of a journey that began four years ago, when Tera met Harris while shooting him in Tokyo for a GQ Japan story in 2022.

Evan Woods / Courtesy of Jeremy O Harris

“Jeremy was in Japan to release his play Daddy,” Tera recalls, “so we did that photo shoot and then just hung out for a month. We went to Fuji Rock, the Coachella of Japan, and just traveled around, and that sparked our friendship.”

Somewhere in that span, Tera mentioned an idea for a movie that he couldn’t stop thinking about, based on a book of portraits of Okinawan youth he’d shot for Marc Jacobs. “He showed me the beginnings of the script and I was like, ‘If there’s any way I can help, let me know,’” Harris says. “So part of our friendship in the years since that initial shoot were these epistolary romance writing sessions. Xavier would send me different drafts and we’d talk about it until we got to the one that we’re at now. It was amazing.”

The resulting film is a lush and sensual coming-of-age story, told in both Japanese and English, that examines the crosscultural tensions intrinsic to Okinawa—an island annexed by Japan in the late 19th century that, since World War II, has housed one of America’s biggest military installations on foreign soil. The Colour of the Sun follows two teens—one Ryukyu, the island’s indigenous culture, and an American living on the base—navigating a complicated relationship. “The backdrop is a little darker,” Tera says, “because obviously the military brings a lot of issues in Okinawa. So that creates a shadow over this friendship, where we see this generational trauma that comes and changes the perception of these two kids toward each other.”

A few days ahead of the premiere, Harris and Tera were spending plenty of time with their film’s young cast, some of whom had never left Okinawa before. “Our star, Naoto [Shimajiri], was standing at the airport in front of a guy who had a sign with his name on it, and he had no idea that it was for him,” Harris says. “He thought we would be there to pick him up.”

Despite that greenness, Harris and Tera had already seen flashes of readiness for the spotlight in their actors—particularly during a fitting for the Maison Margiela looks they’d all be wearing at the festival. “Once they put on the clothes, it was so cool to see how quickly they were able to ease into being movie stars,” Harris says. “There was no hesitation. It was like all of a sudden I saw Yuma [Taira] just putting her hands like this and standing on the carpet already in her head.”

Tera says that Margiela (whose team he also first met through GQ Japan) felt like the perfect choice to represent The Colour of the Sun, which was filmed entirely on 35 millimeter. “Margiela has always been so great at pushing for different textures, and the film is very much about that visually,” he says.

“A movie premiere is a moment when everyone gets to be in a band together,” Harris adds. “You want the band to all show up looking right and playing their parts properly, so you need a designer that is dynamic enough to really show off all of the different colors of the players in your band.” Unsurprisingly, when the crew hit the red carpet on Wednesday night—all glammed up in hair and make-up by Giovanni Errol—their luscious mix of velvets and tweeds and silks looked supremely rock-’n’-roll. (Today, the film was awarded the prestigious FIPRESCI International Critics Prize.)

After the premiere, Harris had planned an afterparty the likes of which La Serenissima had never seen before: a bash at the Palazzo de Fiori complete with sake cocktails, sick custom merch, and DJ sets by the film’s composers, Nosaj Thing and Jacques Greene.

“We’re throwing the craziest rager ever,” he says. “The one negative I have about the Venice Film Festival? Love it, but no one rages here. Because Venice is a very old city, and I feel like people like to go to bed early. But this is going to be a big house party rager that lasts until the wee hours.”
